Exercise 4.4, interiors are open and closures are closed
Exercise 4.5, point-in-polygon classification
contents.reason: Point-location algorithms concern computational classification rather than Jordan content or geometric area, and the area proofs do not query polygon membership algorithmically.

contents.name: Definition 4.6, simple polygons with holes
contents.reason: This pair treats a single simply bounded polygonal region; polygonal domains with holes require oriented boundary bookkeeping and belong with later Green-theorem and planar-domain material.

contents.name: Definition 4.7, triangulation of a simple polygon
Exercise 4.8, necessity of the triangulation intersection conditions
Theorem 4.9, every simple polygon has a triangulation
Exercise 4.10, why the closest interior vertex need not replace the farthest one in the triangulation proof
Theorem 4.11, every nontriangular simple polygon has two nonoverlapping ears
contents.reason: Two ears are useful for guarding and triangulation algorithms, but one interior diagonal already closes the existence proof and the stronger ear count contributes no additional area formula.

contents.name: Theorem 4.12, every triangulation of a simple polygon with more than four vertices contains at least two ears
contents.reason: This structural property of triangulation dual trees supports the art-gallery theorem, whereas the current content-additivity argument needs only pairwise face intersections and finite coverage.

contents.name: Exercise 4.13, proof of the two-ears theorem for a triangulation
contents.reason: The exercise proves the preceding art-gallery-oriented ear result and would duplicate a stronger fact that is not used by any retained plane-area theorem.

contents.name: Exercise 4.14, the shoelace area formula
Lemma 4.15, every triangulation of an n-vertex simple polygon has n-2 triangles and 2n-3 edges
Exercise 4.16, tetrahedralizations of the three-dimensional cube
contents.reason: Three-dimensional tetrahedralization belongs to the separate volume development and is explicitly contrasted by the source with the planar triangulation theorem proved here.

contents.name: Exercise 4.17, an O(n^2) triangulation algorithm
contents.reason: Algorithmic running time is not needed to establish existence, Jordan measurability, or content additivity, and no computational-complexity machinery is declared for this page.

contents.name: Lemma 1.3, elementary incidence properties of a polygon triangulation
Lemma 1.4 (Dehn–Lennes), every simple polygon with at least four vertices has a diagonal
Theorem 1.5 (Dehn–Lennes), every simple polygon has a frugal triangulation
Corollary 1.6, every simple polygon with at least four vertices has an ear
contents.reason: An ear is stronger than the one-diagonal lemma already retained, and the extra shape constraint is not used in the Jordan-content or shoelace derivations.

contents.name: Lemma 1.7, every frugal triangulation of a simple n-gon has n-2 facets and n-3 diagonals
Lemma 1.8, crossing criterion for two diagonals in cyclic vertex order
contents.reason: The cyclic crossing test is useful for triangulation algorithms, but the retained definition already assumes pairwise legal intersections and no proof step constructs a maximal diagonal set.

contents.name: Lemma 1.9, maximal noncrossing diagonals form a frugal triangulation
contents.reason: The existence proof recursively produces a triangulation from a diagonal, so the alternative maximality characterization would duplicate the endpoint without supporting an additional area result.

contents.reason: The current page extends domains by exhaustion while keeping each compact restriction Riemann integrable; unbounded values on a fixed compact set require a separate truncation theory not used by the retained results.

contents.name: Proposition 3.1.20, additivity for nonnegative R# functions
contents.reason: This theorem concerns unbounded-value truncation on a fixed region, whereas all retained improper multiple integrands are locally Riemann integrable and need only domain-exhaustion additivity.

contents.name: Lemma 3.1.21, independence of a nonnegative difference representation
contents.reason: The positive-minus-negative decomposition is canonical in the adopted definition, so the source's more general representation-independence lemma does not discharge a proof obligation here.

contents.name: Proposition 3.1.22, additivity for signed R# functions
contents.reason: Signed additivity for unbounded-value truncations belongs to the broader R# theory; this page needs only locally Riemann-integrable slices and absolute domain exhaustion.

contents.name: Proposition 3.1.23, multiplying a nonnegative R# function by a bounded integrable function
contents.reason: The product theorem is tailored to the source's unbounded-value class, while the Gaussian and domination arguments here use ordinary compact Riemann products and explicit comparison.
